whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Net Zero Cloud Accredited Professional exam for?

personas.label: Sustainability implementers
personas.description: You set up Net Zero Cloud data collection, emissions tracking, and sustainability reports, and want to demonstrate implementation knowledge.

personas.label: Consultants and admins
personas.description: You advise on Scope 1, 2, and 3 accounting and how emissions data is organized for reporting.

personas.label: Career builders

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Net Zero Cloud Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam combines Salesforce configuration with sustainability concepts. Review emissions scopes, data collection, and reporting as well as the platform features.
bullets: 55 scored questions in 75 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
61% to pass, which is 34 correct answers out of 55.
Emissions accounting: Compare Scope 1, 2, and 3 and review how data feeds sustainability reporting.
Practical experience helps: Work through a Net Zero Cloud implementation or configuration example.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Before booking, aim for at least 75% on timed sets and check that you can classify an emissions source, choose a suitable factor, and explain the result. Review Scope 1, 2, and 3 mistakes separately.

examFormat.heading: Net Zero Cloud Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Use the listed exam format to plan a timed practice session, and check the official guide before booking.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: For a scenario, identify the sustainability reporting need and the data available, then compare the proposed Net Zero Cloud solutions.
bestWayToPass: Classify emission sources: Sort examples into Scope 1, Scope 2, or Scope 3 before choosing a reporting setup.
Work through the calculation: Practice multiplying activity data by the right emission factor and compare location-based with market-based Scope 2.
Trace a disclosure report: Know how facility, supplier, and period data flow into the report and how approvals support review.
Check reduction plans: Connect baseline years, targets, reduction actions, and progress measures in a sample scenario.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers using Net Zero Cloud for carbon accounting, including emissions data collection, Scope 1, 2, and 3 tracking, sustainability reporting, and reduction goals. Check Salesforce’s current exam guide for the latest exam logistics.

keyConcepts.h2: Net Zero Cloud AP: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Carbon Footprint Data Model
blocks.body: Net Zero Cloud uses a data model to store sustainability information. Footprint records can track greenhouse gas emissions, energy, water, and waste. Energy Use records track electricity, gas, and fuel by facility and period. Stationary Combustion and Mobile Combustion are Scope 1 sources; Purchased Electricity is a Scope 2 source. Scope 3 data can include business travel, employee commuting, and suppliers. Know how the records connect and how each source is assigned to a scope.

blocks.heading: Emissions Calculations & Emission Factors
blocks.body: Net Zero Cloud calculates emissions by multiplying activity data by an **emissions factor**. For example, a factor converts kilowatt-hours, liters, or miles into kilograms of CO2 equivalent. Factor libraries can provide values from sources such as EPA, IEA, and DEFRA. Companies can use custom factors for measured or supplier data. For Scope 2, location-based reporting uses a local grid average; market-based reporting uses eligible contracts or instruments such as RECs and PPAs.

blocks.heading: Sustainability Reporting & Disclosures
blocks.body: Net Zero Cloud can organize data for sustainability disclosures such as GRI, TCFD, and CDP. Disclosure reports can group footprint data by business unit, facility, or period. Audit trails record submissions and approvals for review. Supplier scorecards summarize supplier emissions and commitments. Targets and milestones track progress toward goals, such as cutting emissions by 50% by 2030. Know how target settings and supplier data feed into reports.

blocks.heading: Data Collection & Integration
blocks.body: Organizations can enter data by hand, upload a CSV, or connect utility, travel, or ERP systems. Utility Data Connections can automate energy data collection. Data quality indicators can flag missing or unusual values. Approval workflows route submissions for review before reports use them. MuleSoft and Salesforce Connect can link data from meters, building systems, and fleet tools. Be able to recognize when data is incomplete or an integration is needed.

blocks.heading: Goals, Targets & Climate Action Plans
blocks.body: Companies can set reduction targets at the organization, business-unit, or asset level. A **baseline year** gives a reference point for measuring progress. Science-based targets align with the 1.5°C or well-below-2°C pathways set by SBTi. Reduction levers record planned and actual actions, such as renewable energy, electric vehicles, or building upgrades. Recalculation rules can adjust baselines after acquisitions, divestitures, or method changes.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Net Zero Cloud Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Practise matching carbon accounting, emissions data, supplier information, and reporting needs to the relevant Net Zero Cloud features.

blocks.heading: Classify Emissions Sources
blocks.body: Map each activity to Scope 1, 2, or 3. Use who owns or controls the source and where the emissions occur.

blocks.heading: Apply Emission Factors
blocks.body: Match each activity unit to the right factor. Compare location-based and market-based Scope 2 methods.

blocks.heading: Check Supplier Data
blocks.body: Scope 3 data may come from suppliers and business travel. Review its source and quality before reporting.

blocks.heading: Track Targets and Actions
blocks.body: Connect the baseline year, target, reduction levers, and progress records so the team can see what is changing.

blocks.heading: Prepare Disclosures
blocks.body: Know how reports group data by site, business unit, and period, and how review records support an audit.

sampleQuestions.question: A company burns gas in its boilers and buys electricity from the grid. Which scopes apply?
options: Gas is Scope 1; purchased electricity is Scope 2.
Both are Scope 2 because the company buys both energy sources.
Both are Scope 1 because the company uses the energy itself.
Gas is Scope 2; purchased electricity is Scope 1.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Gas burned in company equipment is a direct Scope 1 emission. Electricity generated elsewhere is indirect Scope 2.
whyWrong: This correctly classifies the direct gas emissions and purchased electricity.
Scope depends on where the emissions happen, not only whether the energy was purchased.
Purchased grid electricity is Scope 2, not Scope 1.

sampleQuestions.question: Which activities create Scope 3 emissions?
options: Burning gas in a company-owned boiler.
Using diesel in company-owned delivery vans.
Business travel and purchased goods.
Using electricity bought for company buildings.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scope 3 covers value-chain emissions, including business travel and purchased goods.
whyWrong: Gas burned in company equipment is Scope 1.
Fuel burned in company-owned vehicles is Scope 1.
Purchased electricity is Scope 2.

sampleQuestions.question: Why can Scope 3 emissions be difficult to measure?
options: Companies must finish Scope 1 and 2 audits first.
Much of the data is held by suppliers and customers.
There are no methods for measuring Scope 3.
Scope 3 emissions are too small to measure.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scope 3 depends on activity outside the company’s own operations, so supplier and customer data may be hard to collect.
whyWrong: There is no rule requiring Scope 1 and 2 audits before Scope 3 work.
This is a common challenge when collecting value-chain data.
Methods exist for calculating many Scope 3 categories.

sampleQuestions.question: How is an emissions factor used when calculating greenhouse gas output?
options: Converts activity data into an emissions estimate.
Decides which scope an activity belongs to.
Sets the company’s emissions reduction target.
Records what the company paid for its energy.
sampleQuestions.explanation: An emissions factor converts activity, such as kilowatt-hours or fuel use, into estimated greenhouse gas emissions.
whyWrong: This describes the purpose of an emissions factor.
Scope classification depends on the activity and its source.
Targets set a goal; they do not convert activity into emissions.

sampleQuestions.question: A company switches to a supplier that provides renewable electricity. Which reported figure may change?
options: Scope 3 falls because the supplier is in the value chain.
Nothing changes because the electricity still comes through the grid.
Scope 1 falls because the company now generates electricity.
Market-based Scope 2 emissions may fall.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A renewable electricity contract can lower market-based Scope 2 emissions when the matching requirements are met.
whyWrong: A change in electricity supply is not automatically a Scope 3 reduction.
The supplier and contract can affect market-based reporting.
The company still buys electricity; it has not started generating it.

sampleQuestions.question: How do location-based and market-based Scope 2 methods differ?
options: Local grid average vs eligible contract data.
One covers electricity; the other covers gas and other fuels.
One reports the current year; the other reports past years.
One applies to offices; the other to factories.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Location-based reporting uses the local grid average. Market-based reporting uses eligible contracts or instruments.
whyWrong: This describes the two Scope 2 calculation methods.
Both methods apply to purchased electricity, not different fuel types.
They are two methods for calculating the same reporting period.

sampleQuestions.question: A company buys carbon credits to offset some emissions. How should it report them?
options: Leave the offsets out of its sustainability report.
Subtract them from gross emissions and report only the net figure.
Report gross emissions and show offsets separately.
Count them as a reduction in Scope 1 emissions.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Report gross emissions and disclose offsets separately so readers can see both figures.
whyWrong: Offsets should be disclosed even when they are purchased.
Reporting only net emissions hides the gross footprint.
Buying credits does not reduce the company’s own Scope 1 emissions.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does an organization choose a baseline year for its emissions targets?
options: Choosing emission factors for every later year.
Comparing future emissions with a fixed starting point.
Setting the future price of carbon credits.
Assigning activities to Scope 1, 2, or 3.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A baseline year gives the company a starting point for measuring changes in emissions over time.
whyWrong: Emission factors are selected based on the activity and source.
This is the purpose of a baseline year.
Credit prices are set separately from the baseline year.

sampleQuestions.question: A company acquires another business partway through the year. What may need to change in its emissions report?
options: The organizational boundary used for reporting.
Whether business travel counts as Scope 3.
The factors used for the company’s existing activities.
Whether purchased electricity is Scope 1 or Scope 2.
sampleQuestions.explanation: An acquisition can change which operations are included in the reporting boundary.
whyWrong: The reporting boundary may need to include the acquired business.
Business travel remains a Scope 3 category.
Existing activity factors do not change only because of an acquisition.

sampleQuestions.question: Why track emissions per unit of revenue as well as total emissions?
options: Auditors can verify only an intensity figure.
It replaces the need to report total emissions.
It converts emissions into the company’s currency.
Shows emissions intensity as revenue grows.
sampleQuestions.explanation: An emissions intensity measure helps compare efficiency as revenue or business size changes; absolute emissions still matter.
whyWrong: Auditors can review both absolute and intensity measures.
Intensity does not replace absolute emissions reporting.
An intensity measure is not a currency conversion.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a science-based emissions target?
options: A goal based only on the company’s past trend.
A reduction goal aligned with a climate pathway.
A goal audited after the reporting year.
A goal that covers Scope 1 only.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A science-based target aligns a company’s emissions reductions with a climate pathway, such as limiting warming.
whyWrong: Past performance alone does not define whether a target is science-based.
This describes a target aligned with climate science.
An audit is not what makes a target science-based.

sampleQuestions.question: A company knows its electricity use in kilowatt-hours but has no emissions value. What does it need?
options: The electricity bill amount.
An emissions factor for the electricity source.
A new baseline year before any calculation.
A full equipment audit before estimating emissions.
sampleQuestions.explanation: The company needs an emissions factor to convert kilowatt-hours into estimated emissions.
whyWrong: Cost alone does not convert energy use into emissions.
A baseline year is not required for this calculation.
A full equipment audit is not needed to apply a factor to known electricity use.

sampleQuestions.question: Why do carbon accounting teams review data quality so often?
options: Measured data is available for every emissions category.
Industry averages are never allowed.
The law requires every value to be accurate to three decimals.
Many activity values are estimated rather than directly measured.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Some activity data is estimated or incomplete, so teams need to check its quality and document assumptions.
whyWrong: Measured data is not available for every category.
Industry averages may be used where appropriate.
There is no universal three-decimal accuracy rule.

sampleQuestions.question: Employee commuting emissions usually belong to which scope?
options: None; commuting is a private activity.
Scope 2 because it involves purchased energy.
Scope 3 as part of the value chain.
Scope 1 because employees work for the company.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Employee commuting is an indirect value-chain activity and is reported in Scope 3.
whyWrong: Commuting can be included in Scope 3 accounting.
Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased energy used by the company.
Employees commuting in their own vehicles are not company-owned sources.

sampleQuestions.question: A company is starting to measure its carbon footprint. What should it do first?
options: Hire auditors before collecting any data.
Buy credits to offset an initial estimate.
Set its reporting boundary and gather activity data.
Announce a net-zero target before measuring emissions.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Set the organizational boundary and gather activity data before calculating and reporting emissions.
whyWrong: Auditors can review later; the company first needs data to measure.
Credits do not replace measuring the company’s emissions.
The company needs a measured baseline before setting a credible plan.
